According to the Savannah River Ecology Laboratory, brown anoles eat a variety of insects and are among the most abundant reptiles in the areas where they're established.

The brown anole is a brown lizard with patterns on its back, extending into its legs. The pattern has a mixture of white, pale yellow/orange, and dark brown. The pattern appears on both sides of the lizard, becoming lighter as it moves away from the middle, separated by what seems to be its white, raised spine. They have diamond/triangle shaped eyes. They can range from up to 5 to 8.5 inches (12 - 21 cm). This species was found on a stone under a plant, near the ground. The weather outside was warm with little wind. A characteristic that differentiates it from other organisms is the unique pattern on its back. They are originally from the Caribbean, but were introduced to Florida and are slowly entering Georgia.

The Brown Anole, or Anolis sagrei, is a species of lizard in the class Reptilia. Their coloring is predominantly brown and green with yellow accents across the back. The main feature that distinguishes male from female anole is the red fan under their throat. 
They are a highly invasive species in the Southeastern United States but are native to the Caribbean. Their habitats primarily include open wooded or grassy areas, where tree trunks and other vegetation are low for climbing, protection and feeding. Their diets typically consist of small insects, other smaller lizards and small fish. They reproduce sexually and typically live 4-5 years in the wild.

a)	Color, shape and size:
•	Color: The organism observed had a fully brown body with lighter details on its dorsal side extending all the way through the end of its tail. •	Shape: The organism demonstrated bilateral symmetry. It had four legs, two on each side of the body (one in the posterior and one in the anterior side). Each of its feet had five toes. Its limbs were bent, and it was resting.
•	Size: It was a small organism about 4 centimeters long and the tail alone was as long as its body. 
b)	Habitat: The organism was found in a residential space in the city of Weston, FL. It was near a big body of vegetation including trees and ferns. It was also near damp soil. 
c)	Defining characteristics: The organisms moved fast, utilized its four limbs for motion and had a long tail. The organism was taking up sun in order to regulate its body temperature, a diagnostic behavior in reptiles.  A useful distinctive visual characteristic of this specie is the colored line on its dorsal side going from its head to its tail as well as the spots on its rear limbs. Its skin appears dry and scaly.

description:
With Valeri Ponzo; a successful chase of the Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher at Barnes Park in Miami. I left home at 0413 and arrived at Sarasota at 0607. We were underway in Val's car at 0620, stopping quickly for fuel.

Our itinerary for today (and a bit of tomorrow!) was:

0840-0922: Collier County Rest Area, Big Cypress National Preserve -- a potty break followed by an iNat session. I added two birds to my photographed-in-Collier County list: Blue Jay and Boat-tailed Grackle! We each got at least one lifer: Metallic Blue Lady Beetle (Curinus coeruleus), a very cool-looking "bug."

1033-1418: A.D. (Doug) Barnes Park -- a successful chase of the Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher, which I found perched in a Gumbo Limbo at 1103, so it was a rather easy, rather quick lifer. The weather at the start was post-rain (small pockets of rainwater were in the parking lot), overcast, 81 degrees ("feels like" 87), and breezy. I chased a Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher at Fort De Soto Park in Pinellas County on 28 Sep 2000, but missed it. I had no opportunity to chase another, until today. We saw Tim Towles, and we met Alyssa Crittenden and her dad, Jack. After finding the flycatcher, we remained at Barnes for three more hours, photographing other birds, then walking around, looking for life "bugs" and plants. Although the flycatcher was the star of the show, a Philadelphia Vireo (known to be present) that perched conspicuously less than 20 feet away and then preened for three minutes was another highlight. I added three birds to my Miami-Dade bird list, all of them photographed: Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher, Philadelphia Vireo, and Rose-breasted Grosbeak. We did not see the Yellow-green Vireo recorded previously, and seen by at least one birder today, before we arrived.

1510-1822: Markham Park and Target Range, Sunrise -- I suggested to Val that we visit the butterfly garden because I got my life Soldier here when I most recently visited, on 28 Jan 2024. We spent nearly two hours within 300 feet of the parking area before we entered the butterfly garden or walked the trails (!) -- there were lots of "bugs" here. We walked part of the nature trail, which was unwalkable on the side trails due to a lack of maintenance. White Peacocks were everywhere, and Common Cotton Stainer Bugs were surprisingly numerous. I am sure that we both got several lifer plants and "bugs" here.

1834-2008: The Yard House, Sunrise Mills mall -- we enjoyed an absolutely delicious dinner here -- and I got a new Broward County audio-recorded bird in Fish Crow (there were a few hundred in the mall parking lot as we were entering the restaurant).

2008-2318: driving back to Val's. I missed only one turn all day, an achievement in Broward and Miami-Dade counties!

2328-0138 (Sunday): after fueling up Little Red, I arrived back at Spring Hill.

The Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher is the 549th bird species that I have seen outside of captivity in Florida, and the 527th that I have photographed.

Since the Markham butterfly garden and environs consist of many plants cultivated for butterflies, I tried to be careful in the plants I am submitting. If any of my submissions are known to be planted, please mark as captive.
